Happy (Copadichromis pleurostigmoides) is a maternal mouthbrooding cichlid endemic to Lake Malawi, where it occupies the rocky littoral zone and feeds predominantly on zooplankton. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are remarkably small, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.023 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.023 grams], a value derived from the estimated egg dimensions of a congeneric species. These tiny prolarvae remain endotrophic for several days following eclosion, absorbing their yolk reserves before commencing exogenous feeding. The juveniles then enter a rapid growth phase, and field studies indicate that the ultimate total length attained by adults in this species is 14.4 centimeters [Li = 14.4 centimeters]. This maximum size is comparable to that of other medium-sized utaka cichlids that forage in open water, though intraspecific variation is notable across different sampling sites within the lake. The growth trajectory from a neonate weighing just a few hundredths of a gram to a full-sized adult involves a several-thousand-fold increase in body mass, a pattern that is energetically demanding but typical for lacustrine cichlids occupying productive pelagic niches. Researchers have noted that individuals in sheltered bays often reach slightly smaller asymptotic lengths than those in exposed, food-rich habitats.

The onset of sexual maturation in Copadichromis pleurostigmoides occurs at a total length of 11.5 centimeters [Lp = 11.5 centimeters], a size threshold that corresponds closely with the attainment of reproductive viability in many related utaka species. At this developmental milestone, individuals have accumulated sufficient somatic reserves to support the energetic costs of mouthbrooding. The wet weight at puberty for fish reaching this length is 21.4 grams [Wwp = 21.4 grams], as estimated from length-weight relationships established for this genus. This mass at first maturation contrasts sharply with the ultimate wet weight of 41.7 grams [Wwi = 41.7 grams] recorded for fully grown adults, indicating that approximately half of the adult body mass is accumulated after the onset of puberty. Such a pattern suggests that selection favors early reproduction despite continued somatic growth, a life-history strategy common among iteroparous cichlids inhabiting relatively stable tropical environments. Males tend to be slightly larger than females at equivalent stages, although the length-weight relationship remains consistent between sexes.

Reproductive output in this species is modest compared to many substrate-spawning cichlids, which reflects the constraints of buccal incubation. Under the prevailing thermal conditions of Lake Malawi, which maintain a stable water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], females produce approximately 50 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 50 eggs per clutch], a fecundity estimate based on data from the closely related Copadichromis chrysonotus. This clutch size is consistent with the limited buccal cavity volume available for egg retention and larval protection. Females typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year] at this temperature. This low annual frequency, which yields an overall annual reproductive output of 50 offspring per female, stands in contrast to the multiple spawning events observed in some other Lake Malawi cichlids and likely reflects the prolonged period of maternal care during which the female does not feed. The trade-off between clutch size and offspring survival is evident, as mouthbrooding ensures high protection for the developing embryos but limits the total number of young that can be produced per reproductive cycle.

The lifespan of Copadichromis pleurostigmoides has been documented under natural lake conditions, with individuals living in a stable thermal regime of 19 °C [T = 19 °C] reaching a maximum longevity of approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years]. This age-based mortality estimate is derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith annuli analysis conducted across several populations in the southern part of the lake. The value is consistent with the observed lifespan of other medium-sized utaka cichlids and aligns with predictions based on body size and metabolic scaling. Notably, the water temperature of 19 °C is relatively cool for a tropical cichlid, and this may contribute to a somewhat slower metabolic rate and, consequently, a longer potential lifespan than would be expected for a similarly sized fish inhabiting warmer shallow waters. Senescence in this species appears gradual, with older individuals exhibiting reduced body condition and lower reproductive output before eventual natural mortality. The six-year lifespan supports an iteroparous reproductive strategy spread over several breeding seasons.

Comparative studies among Copadichromis species highlight distinct life-history trade-offs shaped by trophic ecology and predation pressure. The wet weight at birth of approximately 0.023 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.023 grams] places the neonates near the lower end of the range for the genus, a trait that may facilitate higher fecundity within the constraints of mouthbrooding. Meanwhile, the ultimate total length of 14.4 centimeters [Li = 14.4 centimeters] and the corresponding maximum adult mass of 41.7 grams [Wwi = 41.7 grams] position this species as a mid-sized planktivore within the utaka guild. The size at puberty, 11.5 centimeters [Lp = 11.5 centimeters], represents roughly 80 percent of the ultimate length, a relatively high ratio that suggests maturation is delayed until a substantial portion of somatic growth is completed. This pattern is interpreted as an adaptation to reduce the risk of reproductive failure in a competitive environment where larger females can brood more eggs and are less vulnerable to gape-limited predators. The wet weight at first maturation is 21.4 grams [Wwp = 21.4 grams], which is approximately half of the final adult mass, underscoring the considerable post-pubertal growth that continues throughout the reproductive lifespan.
